goals: Explain what inscriptions and the Qutab Minar tell us about the Delhi Sultanate

slides.narration: In this part we learn how historians know about the Delhi Sultanate. We list the five dynasties in order, and then study the market regulations and the Deccan expedition of Alauddin Khalji.

slides.heading: Kinds of source at a glance

rows: Inscriptions in Arabic and Persian on monuments
Monuments such as the Qutab Minar
Building style, rulers who built and repaired
Chronicles such as the history by Ziauddin Barani
An author's point of view; check with other evidence

visual.alt: Table of four kinds of source for the Delhi Sultanate: inscriptions, coins, monuments such as the Qutab Minar, and chronicles such as the history by Ziauddin Barani, with what each gives and the care needed

slides.narration: Historians use four kinds of source. Inscriptions in Arabic and Persian on monuments and coins record builders, dates and titles. Monuments such as the Qutab Minar show building style. Chronicles, such as the history by Ziauddin Barani, give an author's account. Each source needs care, and they are best used together.

slides.heading: The Qutab Minar: who built it
bullets: **Begun** by **Qutbuddin Aibak** about **1199**.
**Upper storeys** completed by **Iltutmish**.
**Repaired and raised** later, including by **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** after lightning damage.

rows: Repaired and raised it after lightning damage

visual.alt: Table of the building of the Qutab Minar: begun by Qutbuddin Aibak about 1199, upper storeys completed by Iltutmish, and repaired and raised by Firuz Shah Tughlaq after lightning damage

slides.narration: The Qutab Minar in Delhi was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak about eleven ninety nine. Iltutmish completed the upper storeys. Later, after lightning damage, it was repaired and raised by rulers, including Firuz Shah Tughlaq. So one tower connects rulers of several dynasties.

slides.heading: Features of the Qutab Minar
bullets: About **72.5 m** high.
Built of **red and buff sandstone and marble**.
**Bands of carved inscriptions** and **arches**.
Part of the **UNESCO World Heritage Site** Qutb Minar and its Monuments (**1993**).

rows: Red and buff sandstone and marble
Part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Qutb Minar and its Monuments (1993)

visual.alt: Table of features of the Qutab Minar: about 72.5 m high, red and buff sandstone and marble, bands of carved inscriptions and arches, part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Qutb Minar and its Monuments listed in 1993

slides.narration: The Qutab Minar is about seventy two and a half metres high. It is built of red and buff sandstone and marble, with bands of carved inscriptions and arches. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site called Qutb Minar and its Monuments, listed in nineteen ninety three.

slides.heading: What the Minar tells us
slides.body_md: Read the monument as a source, not only as a sight.

rows: The building style of the Sultanate
Later rulers continued the work of earlier ones

visual.alt: Table of what the Qutab Minar tells us: arches and calligraphy show the building style, inscriptions give builders, dates and titles, and repairs and additions show later rulers continued earlier work

slides.narration: The arches and the calligraphy show the building style of the Sultanate. The inscriptions name builders and give dates and titles. The repairs and additions show that later rulers continued the work of earlier ones. A single building cannot tell the whole story, so we also use coins and chronicles.

visual.caption: The five dynasties (to scale).

slides.narration: The Delhi Sultanate was ruled by five dynasties in turn. They were the Mamluk, also called Slave or Ilbari, the Khalji, the Tughlaq, the Sayyid and the Lodi. The bars are drawn to scale. The Tughlaq dynasty lasted longest and the Khalji dynasty was the shortest. The Lodi line ended at the First Battle of Panipat in fifteen twenty six.

bullets: **Mamluk (Ilbari)**: **1206 to 1290**, begins with **Qutbuddin Aibak**.
**Khalji**: **1290 to 1320**, **Alauddin Khalji** is its best-known ruler.

slides.narration: The Mamluk dynasty ruled from twelve oh six to twelve ninety. It began with Qutbuddin Aibak, and Iltutmish completed the Qutab Minar. The Khalji dynasty ruled from twelve ninety to thirteen twenty. It was founded by Jalaluddin Khalji, and Alauddin Khalji is its best known ruler.

slides.narration: The Tughlaq dynasty ruled from thirteen twenty to fourteen fourteen. The Sayyid dynasty, founded by Khizr Khan, followed until fourteen fifty one. The Lodi dynasty, founded by Bahlul Lodi, ruled until fifteen twenty six, when its last ruler was defeated at the First Battle of Panipat.

slides.heading: Alauddin Khalji and his challenge
bullets: Reign about **1296 to 1316**.
**Mongol raids** made a **large standing army** necessary.
A large army needs money, so **prices** had to be kept low.

rows: Mongol raids and the need for a large army
Market regulations, military and revenue reforms
Deccan expedition led by Malik Kafur

visual.alt: Table about Alauddin Khalji: reign about 1296 to 1316, the challenge of Mongol raids, the answer in market regulations and reforms, and the Deccan expedition led by Malik Kafur

slides.narration: Alauddin Khalji ruled from about twelve ninety six to thirteen sixteen. The Mongols raided repeatedly, so he needed a large standing army. A large army needs steady pay, so he tried to keep prices low, so that modest salaries would be enough for soldiers.

notes.title: The Delhi Sultanate — notes

sections.heading: 1. Sources: inscriptions and the Qutab Minar
sections.body_md:
- **Inscriptions** in **Arabic and Persian** on monuments and coins record **builders, dates and titles**, so they help to fix who built what and when.
- **Chronicles**, such as the history by **Ziauddin Barani**, give an author's account and are checked against other evidence.
- **Qutab Minar (Qutb Minar), Delhi:** begun by **Qutbuddin Aibak** about **1199**; the upper storeys were completed by **Iltutmish**; it was repaired and raised later, including by **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** after lightning damage. It is about **72.5 m** high, built of **red and buff sandstone and marble**, with **bands of carved inscriptions**. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site **Qutb Minar and its Monuments** (1993).
- It shows the **building style** (arches, calligraphy) and the rulers who worked on it.

sections.heading: 3. The dynasties in order
sections.body_md:
- **Mamluk (Slave or Ilbari):** 1206 to 1290, begins with Qutbuddin Aibak.
- **Khalji:** 1290 to 1320, founded by Jalaluddin Khalji; Alauddin Khalji is the best-known ruler.
- **Tughlaq:** 1320 to 1414, founded by Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq.
- **Sayyid:** 1414 to 1451, founded by Khizr Khan.
- **Lodi:** 1451 to 1526, founded by Bahlul Lodi; it ends at the **First Battle of Panipat** (1526).
- Lengths: Tughlaq about 94 years (longest), Khalji about 30 years (shortest).

sections.heading: 4. Alauddin Khalji: market regulations and the Deccan expedition
sections.body_md:
- **Alauddin Khalji** ruled about **1296 to 1316**.
- **Market regulations. Aim:** to maintain a large standing army on modest salaries, especially against Mongol raids. **Measures:** fixed prices for grain, cloth, horses and other goods; separate markets; a market superintendent (**shahna-i-mandi**); state granaries; registration of merchants; spies reporting on traders; strict penalties for cheating on weights. **Results:** stable prices in Delhi during his reign, but the system ended after him.
- **Deccan expedition**, led by **Malik Kafur:** **Devagiri** (Yadavas) about 1307 to 08; **Warangal** (Kakatiyas) about 1309 to 10; **Dwarasamudra** (Hoysalas) about 1311; **Madurai** (Pandyas) about 1311. **Aim:** wealth and tribute rather than direct annexation (mostly). **Results:** great wealth for Delhi; the southern kingdoms accepted overlordship.

key_terms.definition_md: Wealth paid by one ruler to another who is more powerful.
Rule over a ruler who keeps his own kingdom.

sections.heading: 5. Alauddin Khalji: nobility, army and revenue
sections.body_md:
- **Nobility:** feasts and gatherings of nobles only with **permission**; marriages between noble families only with **permission**; a **ban on liquor**; a **spy system**; **grants and gifts of land taken back**.
- **Military reforms:** a **permanent standing army paid in cash**; **dagh** (branding of horses); **huliya or chehra** (descriptive roll of soldiers); **forts strengthened** against the Mongols.
- **Revenue reforms:** **measurement of land**; land tax in the **Doab** raised to about **half of the produce**; collection in **cash or kind**; curbs on the privileges of **khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis**.

sections.heading: 6. Muhammad bin Tughlaq: capital and token currency
sections.body_md:
- **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** ruled about **1325 to 1351**.
- **Transfer of the capital**, about **1327**, from Delhi to **Devagiri**, renamed **Daulatabad**. Reasons commonly taught: a **central location** to control the south and **safety from Mongol raids**. Failure: the **hardship** of the long journey, the **distance from the north-west frontier**, and the return to Delhi.
- **Token currency**, about **1329 to 30**: **bronze or copper coins** valued like **silver tankas**, as commonly taught at a time of **silver shortage**. Failure: **easy forgery**, **loss of trust**, and the coins were **withdrawn and exchanged by the treasury**.

sections.heading: 7. Muhammad bin Tughlaq: the Doab and plans of conquest
sections.body_md:
- **Taxation in the Doab:** the tax increase came at a time of **famine**, which led to **unrest** and the **flight of peasants**. Later **relief measures** (loans, wells) came **late**.
- **Plans of conquest:** **Khurasan**: an army was raised and then **disbanded**. **Qarachil** (Kumaon hills region): an expedition that suffered **heavy losses**.
- **Two views:** some historians regard him as a **far-sighted** ruler whose plans were **poorly carried out**; others regard them as **impractical**.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving a date without the word about, or mixing up the order of the dynasties.
- Saying that Iltutmish began the Qutab Minar (Aibak began it, Iltutmish completed the upper storeys).
- Mixing up the Deccan kingdoms and their dynasties.
- Giving the Alauddin reforms without their aim.
- Writing that the capital moved to Daulatabad for a single reason; give both reasons and the causes of failure.
- Giving only praise or only blame of Muhammad bin Tughlaq instead of both views.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: one correct option, name or term.
- 2 marks: two distinct points; 3 marks: three points.
- 10-mark questions in 3 + 3 + 4 parts: one clear point per mark; the last part usually needs a result, a link or an evaluation.

questions.stem_md: A curator at the imagined Kasara Coin Room finds a worn coin with lettering in Arabic script around its rim. Which question can that lettering help her answer?

options.text_md: How many soldiers the ruler kept in his army
Which ruler issued the coin, with what title, and in which year
What crops were grown in the ruler's kingdom
Which battles the ruler had fought

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Which ruler issued the coin, with what title, and in which year. Inscriptions on coins and monuments record details such as the ruler's name and titles and the date. They do not give army numbers, crops or a list of battles.

questions.stem_md: On a school trip to Mehrauli, the imagined guide Ms. Kavya says: "Work on this tower began about 1199 under the ruler who later became the first sultan of the Mamluk line." Whom does she mean?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Qutbuddin Aibak. Qutbuddin Aibak began the Qutab Minar about 1199. Iltutmish completed the upper storeys, Firuz Shah Tughlaq repaired it much later, and Alauddin Khalji belongs to the next dynasty.

questions.stem_md: A conservation note in an imagined heritage office records that the upper part of the tower was damaged by lightning and later repaired and raised by a Tughlaq ruler. Which ruler does the note refer to?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Firuz Shah Tughlaq. Firuz Shah Tughlaq repaired and raised the Minar after lightning damage. Aibak began it, Ibrahim Lodi was the last Lodi ruler, and Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Class IX club of Gyan Ganga School builds a model of the Qutab Minar at a scale of 1 to 100. The tower is about 72.5 m high. How tall should the model be?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** About 72.5 cm. At 1 to 100 the model is 72.5 m divided by 100, which is 0.725 m or 72.5 cm. A height of 7.25 m would be a 1 to 10 scale, 725 cm is the same 7.25 m, and 7.25 cm would be a 1 to 1000 scale.

questions.stem_md: An imagined quiz card reads: "The Qutab Minar is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site called Qutb Minar and its Monuments." In which year was it listed?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 1993. The site was listed in 1993. The year 2016 is when the ruins of Nalanda were listed, and the other years are distractors.

questions.stem_md: Three imagined students describe what the Qutab Minar tells us. Which statement is the best supported by the monument itself?

options.text_md: Its arches and bands of carved lettering show the building style of the Sultanate, and its long building history connects several rulers
It proves that the whole of India was ruled from Delhi for the entire period
It was finished in a single year by one ruler
It was built only with locally made bricks and no stone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Its arches and bands of carved lettering show the building style of the Sultanate, and its long building history connects several rulers. The Minar's arches, calligraphy and the work of Aibak, Iltutmish and later rulers show a style and a long history. A single building cannot prove rule over the whole country, it was not finished in one year, and it is built of sandstone and marble.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Qutab Minar is only one of several monuments that make up the UNESCO World Heritage Site called Qutb Minar and its Monuments.
questions.solution_md: **True.** True. The listing of 1993 covers the Minar and the other monuments around it.

questions.stem_md: The upper storeys of the Qutab Minar were completed by ___.
questions.solution_md: Iltutmish completed the upper storeys that Qutbuddin Aibak had begun.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A historian in the imagined Salar Library should treat one Persian chronicle of a reign as the complete and final account of that reign.

**Reason (R):** A chronicle reflects the point of view of its author, so it is checked against inscriptions, coins and monuments.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The assertion is false, because no single source gives the complete account. The reason is true: a chronicle, such as the history by Ziauddin Barani, is one author's view and is compared with other evidence.

questions.stem_md: Match each term connected with the sources of the Delhi Sultanate with its meaning.

match_right.text_md: The art of beautiful writing, seen in the bands of the Minar
A written account of events, such as the history by Ziauddin Barani
Writing carved or stamped on stone, metal or a coin
A tower in Delhi begun by Qutbuddin Aibak about 1199

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). An inscription is writing on stone, metal or coins; calligraphy is the art of fine writing; the Qutab Minar is the tower begun by Aibak; a chronicle is a written account of events.

questions.stem_md: Name two kinds of facts that Arabic and Persian inscriptions on monuments and coins give a historian.
questions.solution_md: Any two of: builders, dates, titles.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They record the **builder or issuer**, that is, the ruler or official who ordered the work.
2. They give the **date** and the **titles** the ruler used, which help to place him in time.

questions.stem_md: Explain three things the Qutab Minar tells us about the Delhi Sultanate.
questions.solution_md: Style; inscriptions naming rulers; continuity across rulers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Its **arches and calligraphy** show the building style of the Sultanate.
2. Its **inscriptions** name the rulers who built and repaired it.
3. The work of **Aibak, Iltutmish and Firuz Shah Tughlaq** over many years shows that rulers of different dynasties continued earlier buildings.

marking_scheme.step: Arches and calligraphy as a style

questions.stem_md:
The Qutab Minar in Delhi is one of the best-known sources for the history of the Delhi Sultanate.

(i) Name the ruler who began it, the ruler who completed the upper storeys, and one later ruler who repaired it. **[3]**
(ii) Describe its main features. **[3]**
(iii) Explain what the Minar and its inscriptions help a historian to learn. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Rulers; features; what the Minar and inscriptions reveal.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Qutbuddin Aibak** began the tower about **1199**. **Iltutmish** completed the upper storeys. Later, **Firuz Shah Tughlaq** repaired and raised it after it was damaged by lightning.

(ii) The Minar is about **72.5 m** high and is built of **red and buff sandstone and marble**. It rises in several storeys with balconies and has **bands of carved inscriptions**. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site **Qutb Minar and its Monuments**, listed in 1993.

(iii) The **arches and calligraphy** show the building style of the Sultanate. The **inscriptions** record the builders, dates and titles, so they help fix who ruled and when. Its repair by later rulers shows that the building was valued across dynasties.

marking_scheme.step: (i) A later repairer such as Firuz Shah Tughlaq

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Tughlaq. The order is Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, so the Tughlaq dynasty follows the Khalji. The Mamluk came before it, and the Sayyid and Lodi came later.

questions.stem_md: An imagined timeline in the Meerpur Heritage Room gives the Mamluk dynasty as 1206 to 1290 and the Tughlaq dynasty as 1320 to 1414. Comparing all five dynasties by length, which statement is correct?

options.text_md: The Mamluk dynasty lasted longest, about 94 years
The Tughlaq dynasty lasted longest, about 94 years, and the Khalji dynasty was the shortest, about 30 years
The Sayyid dynasty was the shortest, about 30 years
The Lodi dynasty lasted longest, about 75 years

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Tughlaq dynasty lasted longest, about 94 years, and the Khalji dynasty was the shortest, about 30 years. The lengths are Mamluk about 84, Khalji about 30, Tughlaq about 94, Sayyid about 37 and Lodi about 75 years. So the Tughlaq lasted longest and the Khalji was the shortest.

questions.stem_md: An imagined exhibition panel starts its story of the Delhi Sultanate in the year 1206. Which dynasty began to rule in that year?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Mamluk (Ilbari) dynasty. The Mamluk dynasty, also called the Slave or Ilbari dynasty, began in 1206. The Khalji began in 1290, the Tughlaq in 1320 and the Lodi in 1451.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Delhi Sultanate is said to have ended in 1526.

**Reason (R):** In that year Ibrahim Lodi, the last Lodi ruler, was defeated by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: the defeat of the last Lodi ruler at Panipat in 1526 is the event that closes the Sultanate period.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in chronological order, earliest first.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (e) → (a) → (d) → (c). Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Match each dynasty with the years it is commonly taught to have ruled.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). The Khalji ruled 1290 to 1320, the Tughlaq 1320 to 1414, the Sayyid 1414 to 1451 and the Lodi 1451 to 1526.

questions.stem_md: Name the first and the last dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate and give the year in which each began or ended.
questions.solution_md: Mamluk 1206; Lodi 1526.

answer.model_answer_md: The first was the **Mamluk (Ilbari) dynasty**, which began in **1206**. The last was the **Lodi dynasty**, which ended in **1526** at the First Battle of Panipat.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student writes the order as Khalji, Mamluk, Tughlaq, Lodi, Sayyid. Correct the order and give the starting year of any two of the dynasties.
questions.solution_md: Correct order with two starting years.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The correct order is **Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi**.
2. The **Mamluk** dynasty began in **1206** and the **Khalji** in **1290**.
3. The Sayyid dynasty came before the Lodi, which began in **1451**.

marking_scheme.step: Sayyid before Lodi or a third year

questions.stem_md: The imagined clerk Bharat writes in his ledger: "The Sultan wants goods in Delhi to cost little, so that soldiers on modest pay can still buy what they need." What was the main aim of the market regulations of Alauddin Khalji?

options.text_md: To raise the land tax to half of the produce
To maintain a large standing army on modest salaries, especially against Mongol raids
To move the capital to the Deccan
To issue copper coins valued like silver

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To maintain a large standing army on modest salaries, especially against Mongol raids. The regulations kept prices low so a big army could be paid modest salaries, which mattered during Mongol raids. The land tax, the move of the capital and token coins are other topics.

questions.stem_md: At the imagined cloth market of Sarai Rohan, an officer inspects the stalls and reports on the traders to the Sultan. Which official under Alauddin Khalji does this describe?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The market superintendent (shahna-i-mandi). The shahna-i-mandi supervised the market. Khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis were local intermediaries in the countryside who were involved in revenue.

questions.stem_md: Govind, an imagined horse dealer of Delhi, finds that he may not sell a horse for more than the fixed rate announced for his market. Which policy of Alauddin Khalji explains this?

options.text_md: Branding of horses with the dagh
The measurement of land in the Doab
Price control through the market regulations

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Price control through the market regulations. Fixed prices for grain, cloth, horses and other goods were part of the market regulations. The dagh was for branding army horses, land measurement belonged to the revenue reforms, and token currency was introduced under a later ruler.

questions.stem_md: An imagined museum card on the Deccan expedition says that the army sent south from Delhi under Alauddin Khalji was led by his general. Who was he?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Malik Kafur. Malik Kafur led the Deccan expedition. Ziauddin Barani was a chronicler, Bahlul Lodi founded the Lodi dynasty and Khizr Khan founded the Sayyid dynasty.

questions.stem_md: An imagined student notes that after the campaigns of about 1307 to 1311, the Yadavas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas and Pandyas sent wealth to Delhi but continued to have rulers of their own. What does this suggest about the aim of the expedition?

options.text_md: It aimed at the direct annexation of every southern kingdom
It aimed at moving the capital to the south
It aimed mainly at wealth and tribute, with the southern kingdoms accepting overlordship rather than being annexed directly

questions.stem_md:
Muhammad bin Tughlaq raised the tax in the Doab and planned conquests in the north and north-west.

(i) Describe the tax increase in the Doab and its results. **[3]**
(ii) Describe his plans for Khurasan and Qarachil. **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate his reign: present two views historians hold about him. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Doab tax; Khurasan and Qarachil; two views.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) He **raised the tax** in the **Doab**, the fertile land between the Ganga and the Yamuna, at a time of **famine**. Many peasants could not pay, and this led to **unrest** and the **flight of peasants** from their fields.

(ii) The army raised for **Khurasan** was **disbanded** without a campaign. The **Qarachil** expedition into the Kumaon hills region **suffered heavy losses**. In the Doab, relief measures such as **loans and wells** were taken, but they came **late** to help the peasants.

(iii) **Some historians** regard him as a **far-sighted ruler** whose plans were **poorly carried out**. **Others** see his schemes as **impractical**. A balanced answer says that his ideas had a purpose, but that poor timing and weak preparation caused hardship, so both views deserve a hearing.
